title: Do Premarital Sex Partners Still Reduce Marital Quality? An Update
gist: Reanalyzing General Social Survey data through 2022, sociologist Nicholas Wolfinger finds that having a moderate number of premarital sex partners (up to ~5) no longer reduces marital happiness the way it did in 1989-2016 data, but marriages of the most promiscuous women (21+ partners, 2% of the sample) now show a much steeper happiness penalty than before, a shift he attributes tentatively to generational cohort replacement rather than the COVID-19 shock itself.

themes.theme: Promiscuity-Lite No Longer Hurts Most Marriages

insights.claim: Comparing General Social Survey data from 1989-2016 to 2018-2022, having up to about five premarital sex partners no longer measurably reduces the odds of reporting a 'very happy' marriage for either men or women, whereas in the earlier data any additional partner beyond one was linked to a decline.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A meaningful shift in a decades-old sociological finding: the 'body count' penalty on marital happiness has compressed to only the highest-promiscuity tail, relevant to any thesis about changing marriage-market dynamics and dating-app-era relationship norms.

insights.claim: In the newer data, men with exactly two lifetime sex partners are now a couple of percentage points more likely to report a 'very happy' marriage than men with just one partner — a reversal from the historical pattern where more partners meant lower marital happiness.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A genuinely counterintuitive finding worth flagging: modest premarital sexual experience is now mildly positively associated with marital happiness for men, undercutting simple 'purity culture' assumptions still common in some family-values commentary.
insights.quote: men with two lifetime partners are now a couple of percentage points more likely to report a very happy marriage than are their one-partner peers
insights.locator: The data appear to support my hypothesis

insights.claim: The overall trend in lifetime sexual partners among married Americans is toward more people reporting 'promiscuity-lite' (2-10 partners) and fewer reporting exactly one lifetime partner, while very high promiscuity (way above 10) remains rare but is rising among women and falling among men.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Documents a converging-by-sex trend in premarital sexual behavior — useful background data for any demographic or dating-market analysis of Gen X through Gen Z cohorts.
insights.quote: over time, fewer married people reported one lifetime partner, while more reported what I’ll call promiscuity-lite, between two and 10 partners

themes.theme: The Extremes Are Diverging by Sex

insights.claim: Among the small subset of very promiscuous women (21+ lifetime partners, about 2% of the sample), only 38% report 'very happy' marriages — a steep decline that has no precedent in the older 1989-2016 data, where promiscuity never reduced marital happiness by more than 13 percentage points.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Flags a new and specific at-risk subgroup (highly promiscuous women) whose marital-happiness gap has widened sharply in recent years — a genuinely new finding, not a repeat of prior research, worth watching for replication.
insights.quote: Just 38% of these women report their marriages are very happy.
insights.locator: There’s no such rebound for women

insights.claim: By contrast, the most promiscuous men (21+ partners) report higher rates of 'very happy' marriages (62-64%) than men with 6-20 partners, showing a rebound effect for men that is completely absent for women at the same promiscuity extreme.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A sex-asymmetric finding at the tails of the distribution — useful nuance against any simplistic 'more partners = worse marriage' narrative, since the relationship is non-monotonic for men.
insights.quote: the same can’t be said for the 62%-64% of men with 21+ partners who’re very happy in their marriages
insights.locator: Otherwise, the table suggests little evidence

insights.claim: Only men with 6-10 or 11-20 lifetime partners show a statistically significant reduction in 'very happy' marriage rates versus one-partner men (about 55% vs. 71%); nearly all other partner-count categories, including the concerning 21+ female group, fail to reach statistical significance due to small sample sizes.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: An important caveat for anyone citing these findings: most of the eye-catching extremes (very happy/unhappy at high partner counts) are not statistically robust yet and should be treated as provisional, not confirmed trends.

insights.claim: Controlling for a personal history of divorce, socioeconomic status (income, education), and religiosity (denomination, attendance frequency) does not explain away the relationship between premarital sex partners and marital happiness in either the old or new data — these factors add little explanatory power.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Rules out the most obvious confounders, strengthening the case that whatever is changing the partner-count/happiness relationship is a genuine compositional or cultural shift, not a statistical artifact of who has more premarital sex.
insights.locator: I repeated this analysis for the recent GSS data and found the same thing

insights.claim: Religiosity (denomination and attendance) modestly boosts marital happiness for women but not men, consistent with the author's own earlier research (with Brad Wilcox) finding that more religious women have both fewer partners and happier marriages.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A durable, sex-specific religiosity effect on marital happiness worth incorporating into any model of what predicts marital stability beyond premarital sexual history.
insights.locator: The measures of religiosity—denomination and attendance—together were good for a few percentage points

themes.theme: Cohort Replacement as the Real Driver

insights.claim: The author's leading explanation for why the partner-count/happiness relationship has weakened is generational cohort replacement: the pre-sexual-revolution generations sampled in the 1989-2016 data have been almost entirely replaced by respondents who came of age under different, more sexually permissive norms, a process the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated by disproportionately killing older Americans.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A framework for interpreting many 'norms are shifting' findings in social survey data broadly: apparent behavioral change over time may reflect population replacement (older cohorts dying off) rather than individuals changing their views — useful lens for other longitudinal social-trend analyses.
insights.locator: So, cohort replacement may be changing the relationship between sex and marriage

insights.claim: The author explicitly labels the COVID-19 pandemic an 'exogenous shock' — a rare, system-external event useful for testing whether prior social-science relationships still hold — and frames the pandemic period as a natural checkpoint for revisiting older findings.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A reusable methodological framework (using pandemic-era discontinuities as natural experiments) applicable to reassessing other pre-2020 social or economic relationships that may have shifted due to COVID-driven cohort or behavioral change.
insights.quote: For most of us, the Coronavirus pandemic will be the exogenous shock of our lifetimes

insights.claim: Given small sample sizes at the extremes (e.g., only 192 respondents underlying the 21+-partner women finding, with only marginal statistical significance at p=.05), the author recommends revisiting these findings again in about eight years once more GSS data accumulates.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Sets an explicit low-conviction, long-horizon research checkpoint — a useful marker for tracking whether this finding (women's high-promiscuity happiness penalty widening) replicates or was noise.
insights.quote: it makes sense to update these findings in another eight years
